facts.claim: grandson's "Maria" is a cover of Rage Against the Machine's 1999 song of the same name, which appeared on The Battle of Los Angeles.

The original was written by Rage Against the Machine's members: Brad Wilk, Tim Commerford, Tom Morello and Zack de la Rocha. Kevin Hissink (who records as Boonn) and Taylor Bird are credited as songwriters on grandson's version.
Kevin Hissink, working as Boonn, is credited as co-writer and producer of grandson's 2019 "Maria".

grandson said the aim was to set a story of Mexican migration and indentured servitude against Delta Deep South American blues. He framed this as a comment on slave labor and the perversion of the American Dream.
Loudwire called the cover more somber and bluesy than the heavy, aggressive original. It said the cover still keeps some of the original's attitude and grit.
The cover's video is spliced with audio of President Donald Trump declaring a national emergency to build a wall on the U.S./Mexico border.
The cover had earlier appeared on Rock Sound's 'Worship And Tributes: Volume II' compilation, which came with the magazine's 250th issue.
Rage Against the Machine guitarist Tom Morello remixed grandson's breakout single "Blood // Water" in 2018.
The single is 3:08 long and was released on Fueled by Ramen. Amazon lists its date as May 31, 2019, while Shazam, RYM and AOTY list May 22, 2019.

grandson is Jordan Edward Benjamin, born in Englewood, New Jersey, on October 25, 1993. He grew up mostly in Toronto and began releasing music as grandson in late 2015. He signed to Fueled by Ramen in April 2018.

research.lineage: A bluesy, somber reworking of a 1999 rap-metal protest song, in line with grandson's politically charged alt-rock and rap-rock that Billboard likened to Rage Against the Machine's activist rap-rock.

draft:
The line that changes everything in **Maria** appears twice, almost word for word. Early on, the woman at the center of the song "prays to nothing, no one, nobody, no more." A verse later, bleeding onto a factory floor, the words return with one swap: "I am nothing, no one, nobody, no more." The narrator stops describing her and starts speaking as her. It's a small grammatical move, and it carries the whole song. Faith goes first, then the self.

The story belongs to Rage Against the Machine, who wrote "Maria" for The Battle of Los Angeles in 1999. grandson's version keeps the words and changes the weather. It was co-written and produced by Kevin Hissink, who records as Boonn, with Taylor Bird also credited. grandson said he wanted to set a story of Mexican migration and indentured servitude against Delta Deep South blues, as a comment on slave labor and a perverted American Dream. Loudwire heard it as more somber and bluesy than the heavy original, with some of the grit intact. The lyric already points that way. Maria ends up "Sold and shipped across the new line of Mason Dixon," which ties a modern sweatshop to the old geography of forced work, the same ground the blues came out of.

The sound earns that link without turning into a museum piece. A distorted guitar works a wah-pedal riff over a simple, driving bass line and drums that lean hard on the snare. A clean guitar threads arpeggios through it, a cooler color against the dirt. The room feels mid-sized and unpolished, close and gritty. grandson sings raw and a little strained, with no harmonies to soften anything. The delivery is direct. He sounds less like he's performing outrage than like he's giving testimony.

What he reports is brutal and exact. There's a truckbed and a cross clutched in a fist. There's a quota, and a sewing needle tearing through denim an inch from a vein while the foreman's footsteps pound in her head. The writing tracks her body's panic and then its numbness, the other women gathering and screaming while she watches her own blood like it belongs to someone else. Then the song drops the narrative for a chant: no minutes to rest, no moment to pray, the work eclipsing the day, the plea shrinking to a single moment. The refrain about tearing away the mask keeps coming back, part demand and part exhaustion. Nothing resolves. Her anger and her emptiness stay in the same room.

The cover's video splices in audio of Donald Trump declaring a national emergency to build a border wall, which pulls a twenty-year-old song into the present tense.

You come away holding the moment Maria stops being "she" and becomes "I," and you can't hand her back.

factCheck.claim: The woman 'prays to nothing, no one, nobody, no more' early in the song
factCheck.note: Matches the lyric exactly. It falls in the first verse.

factCheck.claim: 'I am nothing, no one, nobody, no more' returns a verse later 'with one swap'
factCheck.note: The quote is exact. More than one word changes ('She prays to' becomes 'I am'), so 'one swap' became 'in the first person'.

factCheck.claim: She is bleeding onto a 'factory floor'
factCheck.note: The lyrics say blood goes 'to the floor' and mention a foreman and a quota. They never say 'factory'. Now just 'the floor'.

factCheck.claim: Rage Against the Machine wrote 'Maria' for The Battle of Los Angeles in 1999
factCheck.note: Supported: a 1999 original that appeared on The Battle of Los Angeles, written by the band's members. 'Wrote for' was softened to 'appeared on'.
Nothing shows the cover's lyrics are identical to the original. Hissink and Bird are credited as songwriters on the cover.

factCheck.claim: Co-written and produced by Kevin Hissink (Boonn), with Taylor Bird also credited
factCheck.note: Supported by the Shazam and Wikipedia items.

factCheck.claim: grandson said the aim was Mexican migration and indentured servitude set against Delta Deep South blues, as a comment on slave labor and a perverted American Dream
factCheck.note: Kerrang. Wording tightened to attribute it to grandson without a pronoun.

factCheck.claim: Loudwire heard it as more somber and bluesy than the heavy original, with some grit intact
'Sold and shipped across the new line of Mason Dixon'
factCheck.note: Exact lyric. The reading that it ties a modern sweatshop to older forced labor is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: The Mason-Dixon geography is 'the same ground the blues came out of'
factCheck.note: Unsupported history claim. grandson cited the Delta Deep South, not the Mason-Dixon line.

factCheck.claim: Distorted guitar with wah-pedal riff, simple driving bass, drums with prominent snare, clean guitar arpeggios
factCheck.note: Wah is in passes 1 and 3. The other elements are in all three passes.

factCheck.claim: Room feels mid-sized, unpolished, 'close and gritty'
factCheck.note: Mid-sized is in passes 1 and 3. Raw and unpolished is in all three. Gritty is in passes 2 and 3. 'Close' appears only in pass 2, so it was dropped.

factCheck.claim: Vocal is raw and a little strained, direct, no harmonies
factCheck.note: Raw and strained are in passes 1 and 3. Direct is in passes 1 and 2. No harmonies is in all three. 'He' was removed because the singer's gender can't be assumed from the sound.

factCheck.claim: Sounds like giving testimony rather than performing outrage
factCheck.note: Interpretation resting on the direct, unadorned delivery.

factCheck.claim: A truckbed and a cross 'clutched in a fist'
factCheck.note: Lyric says 'clutching her cross'. 'In a fist' was invented and is removed.

factCheck.claim: A quota, a needle through denim an inch from a vein, the foreman's footsteps pounding in her head, the sisters gathering and screaming, eyes on her blood, numbness
factCheck.note: All drawn from the lyrics. Reading of numbness and detachment is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: The song moves to a chant about no rest and no moment to pray, with a recurring 'tear away the mask' refrain
factCheck.note: Shown by the lyrics' structure and repetition.
